ideas.title: A small, generic editorial-rule change can flip the editorial hierarchy and derail an output pipeline
ideas.description: Adding a single reusable instruction — “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis” — to the Narrative user prompt caused the pipeline to subordinate company identity and audience scope and to make orchestration the central message, producing consistently worse Narrative and Compose scores and a decision to rollback.
ideas.audience: Prompt engineers, narrative designers, content ops and product communications leads responsible for AI-assisted content pipelines.
ideas.rationale: This experiment provides direct evidence that even a short, generic editorial instruction can change model behaviour in a stable, repeatable way that matters for publishable output. Teams that modify narrative prompts need objective, task-specific validation (rubrics, multiple runs, gated criteria) because surface-preserving language alone can unintentionally reweight themes and introduce unsupported claims.
ideas.evidence:
- Candidate prompt change: added section titled “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis.” (prompt-changes/Narrative.user.prompt.diff).  
- Only Narrative.user.prompt.txt changed; all other prompt files and inputs identical.  
- Narrative mean score: Baseline 6.00/10 vs Candidate 4.00/10.  
- Compose mean score: Baseline 5.67/10 vs Candidate 3.33/10.  
- Candidate runs uniformly lowered A (identity/audience) scores and failed C (theme hierarchy) — orchestration became central in all candidate runs.  
- Decision: Do not promote; production prompt restored byte-for-byte to baseline (restored SHA-256 matches baseline).

ideas.title: Factual-restraint must be a hard promotion gate — the experiment shows it decides promotion
ideas.description: The candidate prompt consistently introduced unsupported audience framings, validation commitments, or claims; the experiment treats factual/editorial restraint as a hard gate and refused promotion when that gate failed.
ideas.audience: Product managers, compliance editors, release reviewers, and anyone owning promotion criteria for generative content prompts.
ideas.rationale: When model outputs can invent or overclaim, a strict factual-restraint gate prevents publishing unsupported assertions. This experiment demonstrates that failing a factual-restraint criterion is decisive for non-promotion even when other readability or coherence measures are acceptable.
ideas.evidence:
- Scoring rubric: D — Factual/editorial restraint — defined as a hard promotion gate.  
- Narrative runs: several baseline runs scored 0–1 on D; all candidate runs scored 0 on D (introduced validation intent/commitment or audience claims).  
- Compose runs: candidate outputs repeated or extended unsupported additions; no candidate run passed the D gate.  
- Promotion decision explicitly cites failure of the factual restraint gate: “Candidate was worse... failed the orchestration hierarchy and factual restraint gates in every run.”

ideas.title: A generic ‘preserve intent’ instruction can dilute source-specific emphasis (audience and company identity)
ideas.description: The candidate’s added generic editorial rule lacked story-specific wording and, instead of protecting the original emphasis, caused the pipeline to downweight Nuëyon’s company-level identity and target audience while amplifying technical themes.
ideas.audience: Prompt authors, narrative prompt reviewers, editorial leads shaping system prompts for specific brand messages.
ideas.rationale: This shows that editorial rules must be context-sensitive: a broadly worded preservation rule does not guarantee preservation of the particular subject hierarchy present in a given Synthesis. Teams should test whether generic guardrails actually preserve the intended emphasis for each use case.
ideas.evidence:
- Prompt change described: a generic section titled “Preserve Editorial Intent from the Synthesis” that “contains no Nuëyon-specific wording.”  
- Narrative A (identity/audience) scores: Baseline runs mostly A=2; Candidate runs A=1 consistently.  
- Compose outputs: candidate prose “did not restore the intended editorial hierarchy” and “omitted or diluted the audience scope.”  
- Candidate runs made orchestration central despite the intended company-first framing in the baseline.

ideas.title: The experiment demonstrates disciplined, reproducible prompt-change practices (hashing, baseline reuse, rollback)
ideas.description: The report documents a rigorous workflow for prompt experiments: baseline reuse, byte-for-byte prompt snapshots and SHA-256 hashes, controlled runs, saved outputs, and a deterministic rollback when the candidate failed.
ideas.audience: ML Ops engineers, experimentation leads, and engineering managers who govern prompt-change processes.
ideas.rationale: Well-documented, reproducible experiment practices reduce risk when changing prompts in production. This run shows operational controls (hashing, baseline reuse, saved logs, and automated rollback) that made the non-promotion decision auditable and reversible.
ideas.evidence:
- Repo verification: commit be882989a7b7…; baseline user prompt SHA-256 475A9DB1CA028EBC9…; input and prompt snapshots hash-checked.  
- Baseline reuse: three baseline runs reused from prior experiment to preserve conditions.  
- Candidate changes limited to one prompt file; full console logs and outputs saved under baseline/outputs and candidate/outputs.  
- Rollback verification: production prompt SHA-256 restored to baseline value; no commit/push made.

ideas.title: Internal tension in the baseline Synthesis (company identity vs. orchestration) is a fragile point that can be amplified by prompt edits
ideas.description: The baseline Synthesis emphasized Nuëyon’s company identity and Compose as a first product, but it also contained a later phrase calling orchestration “central to the product direction.” That internal tension may have lowered the prompt’s resilience to edits and allowed a small candidate change to shift emphasis toward orchestration.
ideas.audience: Editorial strategists, narrative authors, and prompt maintainers concerned with message consistency across a pipeline.
ideas.rationale: Identifying and removing or clarifying internal contradictions in source briefs or Synthesis content reduces the chance that minor prompt edits will amplify a secondary theme and change the final messaging hierarchy.
ideas.evidence:
- Report text: “The baseline Synthesis pairs company identity with Compose in its top-level emphasis, but also contains a later description calling orchestration ‘central to the product direction.’ That internal tension may have reinforced the technical angle.”  
- Candidate outputs indeed amplified orchestration relative to company identity, consistent with the described tension.  
- The report notes this observation but does not claim it caused the failure (explicitly marked as a possibility).

ideas.title: Experimental limitations matter for statistical claims but not for operational decisions here
ideas.description: The experiment is limited (three runs per condition, no temperature/seed control, potential backend variability under the model alias), which constrains statistical significance; nonetheless, the candidate produced consistent regressions across runs sufficient for a conservative operational decision.
ideas.audience: Research leads, decision-makers evaluating the strength of experimental evidence for prompt changes.
ideas.rationale: Understanding methodological limits prevents overclaiming statistical significance while still enabling pragmatic decisions when failures are consistent and violate hard promotion gates.
ideas.evidence:
- Limitations section: small sample (three runs), no seed or temperature override, model alias backend may change, Idea and Research outputs vary between runs.  
- Despite limitations, candidate runs were consistent in failing key gates (C and D) and produced lower means, which the team judged sufficient to reject promotion.
